prize_parts.citation: For the development of ligand-controlled palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B046 with Buchwald and Hartwig. The reaction replaced narrow, harsh aryl amination with a general catalytic method whose scope comes from ligand design. Bulky, electron-rich phosphine and carbene ligands control oxidative addition, amine binding and reductive elimination, and suppress beta-hydride elimination. That is a mechanistic idea as well as a procedure. It has been confirmed independently for about three decades and is used daily in pharmaceutical, agrochemical and materials synthesis, so maturity is not in question. Buchwald and Hartwig built complementary general systems in parallel, with their own mechanistic work, which gives a clean two-person credit. Of the shortlisted candidates, this one has the fewest open questions on maturity and attribution together. The open question is conceptual distance from 2010, and I think the citation can answer it: the prize is for controlling catalytic C-heteroatom bond formation through ligand architecture, not for cross-coupling in general.
statement.case_against: The 2010 overlap remains the strongest objection. A colleague who values new principles over enabling methodology can fairly say that C-N coupling extends a recognised catalytic cycle to a new nucleophile. Excluding Kosugi and Migita (tin-amide coupling) and Guram and Rennels (contemporaneous work) is a judgement that generality, not first observation, is what the prize rewards. That judgement is defensible but it is a judgement, and the Committee should state it openly. B014 has the stronger novelty claim, with the opposite problem on credit and clinical maturity.

responses.point: Aili holds that B014 adds a new pharmacological principle, that the approved cereblon glues answer the maturity worry, and that B046 is only a fallback on credit clarity.
responses.response: I accept that the cereblon strand is clinically proven and mechanistically explained, and that Handa's work is the strongest answer to the missing PROTAC approval. That narrows my maturity objection but not my credit objection. Your trio of Crews, Deshaies and Handa joins a heterobifunctional design concept to a molecular-glue mechanism, and I am not convinced that the two strands are one achievement. If they are two, a three-name cap forces a citation that omits Ciulli, Ito, Gray and Sakamoto from a prize whose citation names a combined field. On novelty I concede more than in round 1: C-N coupling is closer to 2010 than degraders are to anything previously recognised. What keeps me on B046 is that its credit and maturity can be defended without qualification. If a one-sentence citation for B014 can be agreed that names one strand only, I would reconsider.

responses.point: Linke prefers B027 (Car and Parrinello) for its unambiguous two-author credit and four decades of use, and discounts the 2013 and 2024 computational prizes.
responses.response: I still regard B027 as the best-attributed candidate and I keep it as an alternative. My reservation is the ratio of consequence to recency of recognition. Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics is a foundational method whose influence is mostly on other methods and on materials and condensed-phase simulation. C-N coupling changes what synthetic chemists make on a bench every day. Having two computational prizes in the past thirteen years is not an argument against B027 by itself, but it does weaken the claim that the field is under-recognised. If the Committee wants an award in theory this year, I would not object strongly to B027, but I would not rank it above B046.

responses.point: Zou agrees on B046 and on excluding Kosugi, but asks that the Migita, Guram and Rennels history be checked before the citation is fixed and that the wording say catalytic C-N cross-coupling.
responses.response: I agree that the precedence history is from memory for both of us and that no file provided here lets us verify it. I have adopted your suggestion in my citation, with wording that points to ligand control so the 2010 distinction is visible in the text. I would add that the Committee need not decide whether Kosugi's tin-amide reaction was first. It needs to decide whether the prize rewards the general catalytic method, and that is how I think the citation should be written.

responses.point: Aqvist backs B014 with Crews, Deshaies and Handa as the only way to fit both the PROTAC and cereblon strands into three names, and names B027 as the cleaner fallback.
responses.response: Your coverage argument is a good one: putting Handa beside Crews and Deshaies links a design concept to a clinically proven mechanism. It also shows that any cut here is a choice between strands rather than a clean attribution, and your own file lists Ciulli, Gray, Sakamoto, Ito and Kim as having decisive contributions. I think a prize that the community will read as leaving out half the field is a weaker choice than one with two names that nobody disputes as the inventors of the general method. I agree with you that B027 is a cleaner fallback than B014 if attribution cannot be settled.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee accepts that ligand-controlled C-N coupling is conceptually distinct from the 2010 C-C cross-coupling prize; my view depends on the citation wording.
The Kosugi, Migita, Guram and Rennels precedence is from memory, not verified from the provided files.
Whether the PROTAC and cereblon strands of B014 can be set out as one achievement with a defensible three-name credit; if so, my ranking of B014 would rise.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal. None of the credited names is documented as connected to Lund, Chalmers, KTH, Tartu or Masamune. As the only synthetic organic chemist on the Committee I am closest to B046 and have tried to weigh the objections from colleagues in other fields at full strength.
